data.title: Asean must counter economic nationalism with deeper integration, wider partnerships: DPM Gan
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Asean must counter rising economic nationalism with deeper integration and wider partnerships, in a world where governments are placing more emphasis on self-reliance and control over critical industries, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong on Nov 27.

“Raising barriers among ourselves would narrow the opportunities available to each of us,” he said. A more integrated Asean would strengthen its value as a partner, while broader tie-ups open up more opportunities for the region.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), was delivering a keynote speech at SPH Media’s Asia Future Summit 2026, jointly presented by The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

The annual event gathered policymakers, business leaders and industry experts, with OCBC as the presenting sponsor, Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his speech, Gan identified three factors that make integration and partnerships especially important: artificial intelligence, geopolitical shocks and geo-economic contestation. “Each can strengthen the impulse to turn inward. Yet each also makes cooperation more crucial,” he said.

His remarks followed the United States’ announcements of fresh tariffs and chip export restrictions over the past two weeks, moves which affected many in South-east Asia as the region finds itself in the crosshairs of sharpening rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

“Geo-economic competition is reshaping the networks through which we trade, invest and access technology,” Gan said, with governments paying closer attention to dependencies and control over critical capabilities.

“Asean countries cannot determine how major powers manage their differences,” he added. “But we can maintain relationships across these divides and remain a bridge for trade, investment and cooperation.”

Doing so would require that Asean earn and sustain its partners’ confidence in the grouping’s integrity, institutional reliability and business environment by issuing clear and predictable rules, upholding its laws and commitments, and taking firm action against wrongdoing, he said.

“As scrutiny of international trade and investment intensifies, maintaining these standards becomes even more important,” he added.

ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary in 2027, with Singapore pushing for deeper integration and wider partnerships as it takes on Asean’s rotating chairmanship at a time of heightened geopolitical contestation.

Both the US and China would continue to be key economic partners for Asean, Gan said, with their businesses, technologies and markets important to the region’s growth.

Both countries are among the region’s largest trading partners and sources of foreign direct investment.

In tandem, the grouping is strengthening tie-ups with other partners that would expand the region’s economic options and reduce its exposure to disruptions, Gan said.

These include negotiations to upgrade Asean’s trade agreements with South Korea and Canada, moves to expand and enhance the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and growing links with other regional groupings such as the European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Asean is also strengthening integration within the grouping, with Gan highlighting recent efforts that would help firms better tap suppliers and customers within the region.

A recently upgraded Asean Trade in Goods Agreement, set to be rolled out in end-2026, will help businesses reduce costs through streamlined procedures and more transparent rules, he said, while a customs-related mutual recognition arrangement would give trusted traders faster clearances and priority treatment in participating countries.

And a regional Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed earlier in the month would make cross-border transactions, payments and access to digital services easier, he added.

These would make Asean more valuable as a place to produce and market to serve, and form a stronger regional base enabling the grouping to “engage the world with greater confidence”, Gan said. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: AI here to stay despite tech bifurcation: OCBC chief Tan Teck Long
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Falling artificial intelligence costs are continuously lowering the hurdle for corporates to boost productivity, and will lead to readier and wider use of AI in the years ahead, OCBC group CEO Tan Teck Long said on Friday (Nov 27).

Speaking at the Asia Future Summit 2026, amid a global tech rout fuelled by concerns over AI investment, Tan said AI is here to stay. “Despite the current worries about AI-related stocks, AI is here to stay given increased adoption, improved AI model capability and declining cost of AI.”

The OCBC chief was delivering the opening address at the annual thought leadership conference, which returned for its fifth edition this year.

For the first time, it was jointly presented by SPH Media’s key news titles: The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

OCBC is the presenting sponsor, with Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

In his opening remarks, he noted Asia’s role in shaping supply chains and how AI is used.

While AI adoption may become more widespread, the technology landscape supporting that adoption could become more fragmented.

The future is likely to see bifurcation in technology standards, differentiated access to technology and possibly AI models, he said.

The way he sees it, the optimal path forward – balancing cost and security considerations – appears to be a mix of open and closed-source models.

Open-source ones, which many Chinese AI models are, allow users to bring them on premise and customise them to their needs, he said.

Closed-source ones, which are more common among American AI models, may be fast to set up, but are a black box to users, he continued.

But Tan maintained that technological bifurcation does not mean complete supply chain separation. “Even as technology controls tighten, the underlying supply chain remains deeply connected.”

He added that, despite trade tariff disruptions, intra-Asia trade remains on the rise and accounts for more than half of the region’s total trade. Likewise, foreign direct investment into Asean continues to grow, anchored by supply chain diversification and AI-driven investments.

Regional trade agreements and collaboration will be key to sustaining this growth momentum, he said.

Digital-green convergence

AI can also be leveraged to promote green energy, noted Tan.

“When OCBC finances data centres, we note that tech companies are increasingly demanding clean energy to meet sustainability goals,” he said. “Data centres are very power hungry and those supporting AI even more so.”

Whether existing power grids can support all the demand remains to be seen.

But, in the data centre world, it is increasingly about bringing your own power, and such demand can help to spur the development of green energy, he said.

Tan raised the example of how OCBC provides green financing for a Singapore data centre pioneering a hydrogen energy proof-of-concept, as well as for data centres using solar energy.

Heightened cyber threats

But, as AI adoption grows, so do the risks of exposure to heightened cyber threats and scams, he contended.

He pointed to investment scam losses in Singapore, which totalled S$170 million in the first half of the year and accounted for some 40 per cent of total scam losses. Such scams are the costliest category by dollar amount, he noted.

OCBC is helping to lead the banking industry’s fight against scams, said the bank chief.

Collective efforts have made a difference, as total scam losses fell 18 per cent in the first half of the year while investment scams declined 5 per cent, he pointed out.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson Holdings, Hongkong Land, Marco Polo Marine
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 27):

Jardine Matheson Holdings (JMH) , Hongkong Land : JMH announced on Thursday that Adam Keswick – whose family controls the Jardine group – will step down from the board effective Dec 31, 2026. He will also step down from the board of Hongkong Land. JMH ended Thursday at US$60.38, up US$0.25 or 0.4 per cent, while Hongkong Land was US$0.07 or 0.8 per cent higher at US$8.53, before the announcement.

Marco Polo Marine : The marine logistics company posted on Friday a 56 per cent drop in net profit to S$21.3 million for its second half ended Sep 30, 2026, from S$47.9 million in the previous corresponding period. Revenue for H2 rose 11 per cent to S$78 million from S$70.1 million. Earnings per share stood at S$0.0055 for the half-year period, down from S$0.0128. Shares of Marco Polo Marine ended at S$0.093 on Thursday, S$0.005 or 5.7 per cent higher.

data.title: Bank of Singapore rolls out private-markets strategy with iCapital
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Bank of Singapore has introduced a new private-markets strategy for its clients, expanding their access to alternative investments beyond hedge funds.

Developed in partnership with fintech platform iCapital, the proprietary strategy is available within eligible discretionary portfolio management mandates, the OCBC private-banking arm announced on Friday (Nov 27).

The bank plans to extend the offering to advisory clients in 2027.

The strategy allocates across private equity, private credit, private real estate and private infrastructure, with the aim of providing clients broader diversification beyond public markets.

The launch reflects growing client demand for private assets.

“Over the past three years, clients’ AUM (assets under management) allocated to private assets have increased by close to 60 per cent, reflecting the growing appetite for resilient, long-term investment opportunities beyond public markets,” said Jean Chia, global chief investment officer at Bank of Singapore.

Under the tie-up, Bank of Singapore will oversee strategic capital allocation and investment management. iCapital will supply the technology and platform to support the delivery of the mandate.

Brooks Entwistle, head of international at iCapital, described the offering as a “bespoke solution” that “allows the bank to stay focused on what matters most: its investment decisions and client outcomes”.

“Over time, we see the potential for this infrastructure to support a broader range of wealth management client segments across the OCBC Group network,” Entwistle added.

data.title: Trump says Huang excited about his ‘second term’ at Nvidia
data.description:
PRESIDENT Donald Trump said Jensen Huang is looking forward to his “second term” as chief executive officer of Nvidia, reiterating his praise for the man whose reinstatement he pushed hard for despite bipartisan backlash over national security concerns.

Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Thursday (Nov 26), the president said he has not spoken to Huang since Nvidia announced his return, but probably will at some point.

“When I did speak to him, he is so happy to be going back. He calls it his second term,” Trump said.

The president again dismissed national security concerns over the reinstatement of Huang, who was ousted after revelations that he had extramarital affairs including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. 

“Based on information and belief, I think he’s absolutely fine,” Trump said. Pressed on what information he had, he did not give a specific answer, only saying, “The information I have, which is a lot of information.”

Nvidia earlier this week restored Huang as CEO, following intervention from Trump, who also enlisted Vice-President JD Vance to help make a personal appeal to the board. Trump told CNBC on Monday he spoke to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” and “felt very strongly” that Huang should be brought back.

Trump’s efforts drew widespread criticism from both Republicans and Democrats, with lawmakers vowing to investigate ties between Huang and the Trump administration.

Huang is set to testify to House lawmakers behind closed doors on Dec 1, and then publicly before the Senate on Dec 3.

Nvidia’s stock soared more than 31 per cent on Monday after the announcement of Huang’s return, but lost more than 9.5 per cent in the next two days. The US market was closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.

“I will tell you, the market feels very good about it,” Trump said. “I was a little concerned yesterday when I saw some pretty big dips, and by the end of the day, it was it was up again. So I really did, I think I did a great thing for our country and even for the world.”

Trump is due to travel on Dec 4 to Arizona to headline a groundbreaking event for a Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp chip manufacturing plant expansion — a facility that produces chips for Nvidia. 

The president said he hadn’t considered whether Huang should join him, but added: “I would be glad to take him.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Cautious consumers gear up for Black Friday as inflation woes bite
data.description:
[NEW YORK/LOS ANGELES] Neither high fuel prices nor stubborn inflation are expected to stop US shoppers from spending robustly as their turkey hangovers wear off on Black Friday. But below healthy top-line forecasts lie signs of stress.

Holiday spending — which unofficially begins on Black Friday — is seen topping last year’s strong figures by 4 to 6 per cent, several economic forecasts show. But most of the gains will be attributable to inflation which, at 3.8 per cent, is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years.

The National Retail Federation sees November-December holiday retail sales rising 4.2 per cent year-over-year, to just above US$1 trillion. The Mastercard Economics Institute and EY Parthenon each forecast sales to rise more than 5 per cent.

Eventual final results often beat pre-holiday estimates. Still, consumer sentiment remains shaky. This month, voters punished US President Donald Trump for an Iran War that’s pushed the cost of living higher, handing Democrats sweeping electoral victories.

A November survey by the National Retail Federation found that 82 per cent of consumers are taking steps to manage holiday costs, like buying less expensive gifts.

Los Angeles resident Felicia Cox, 50, said that while her holiday spending will be roughly stable, inflation is impacting how she thinks.

“I want to get more gifts that people will actually use or need,” said Cox, a sales representative, while browsing in an L.A. Marshalls last week. “I feel like people aren’t able to afford as much stuff.”

Worries aside, some 87 per cent of 1,200 consumers surveyed by Deloitte in October planned to participate in the five-day shopping period from Thanksgiving through “Cyber Monday”, Nov 30 — the highest in a decade, according to Deloitte.

“People like to spend during the holidays,” even when there’s a “persisting undercurrent of stress,” said Katie Thomas, who leads the Kearney Consumer Institute, part of global consulting firm Kearney.

Middle- and lower-income shoppers — who have been trading down for months — were however more likely than wealthy ones to spend less, according to the Kearney survey.

Target, Dollar Tree and Kohl’s have all pointed to belt-tightening during recent earnings calls. Kohl’s CEO Michael Bender on Tuesday cited an “increasingly choiceful” consumer that is “looking to stretch every dollar.”

Holiday spending forecasts mostly predated the recent stock market correction that followed the midterms, turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, and mounting concerns around an AI bubble.

The decline could dampen the wealth effect that has seen affluent shoppers splurge on gadgets and accessories, UBS analysts said in a note on Tuesday.

Toys take a hit

Higher input costs, particularly from petrol derivatives like plastic, are hitting some products more than others.

Prices of toys — generally high in plastic — have risen 13.2 per cent since the start of the year, pushing Barbie maker Mattel this month to cut its annual forecast as consumers balked at higher costs.

Some unlikely products are buoying the toy category. Best Buy and Target have both flagged trading cards — including Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering products — as a key growth driver. Squishy NeeDoh toys were selling for US$24.99 on Amazon in October, nearly triple the price a year earlier on hot demand, according to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend.

Toy maker Learning Resources Inc — a plaintiff in lawsuits that overturned Trump’s tariffs — is seeing demand roughly flat, said CEO Rick Woldenberg, though he added it’s hard to predict demand before Black Friday.

“People can’t shop until they have their turkey,” Woldenberg said.

AI could also scramble the year’s shopping dynamics.

As shoppers use AI to find bargains or even complete purchases — and retailers become increasingly adept at altering price quickly through AI — the deepest discounts could come closer to Christmas, as consumers and retailers both wait out the market, said Ryan Orabone, a consultant at Spaulding Ridge.

“My advice to shoppers is to be patient,” he said. “Don’t jump on the first deal you see.” REUTERS

data.title: Schroders expands wealth management business to Asia amid uptick in generational wealth transfers
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Schroders Wealth Management has brought its global wealth advisory services to the Asia-Pacific amid a growing number of families in the region that require help navigating generational wealth transition processes.

Regional wealth transfers are set to accelerate with around US$5.8 trillion of wealth estimated to change hands in Asia by 2030.

Clients these days increasingly have an asset footprint beyond their country of origin – where family members and their wealth are well distributed around the world, said James Gladstone, head of wealth planning at Schroders Wealth Management.

“That does present a challenge, in terms of how they manage or structure their assets…in tax efficient and compliant ways across different jurisdictions,” he said in an exclusive interview with The Business Times.

The expansion of Schroders’ wealth management arm to Asia complements work in other bases – in the Middle East and United Kingdom – to better support their pool of high-net-worth (HNW) and ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) clients.

However, even as Singapore and Hong Kong continue to account for a significant share of Schroders’ Asian client base, the move has fuelled growing demand for advisers specialising in India and the broader North Asian markets.

These areas have been identified as “growth markets”, where the Asia wealth advisory service hopes to build capabilities, said Evonne Tan, Schroders Wealth Management’s Asia chief executive officer.

Singapore will be the regional hub for Schroders’ wealth advisory in Asia.

Alvin Chiam, head of wealth advisory, Asia at Schroders Wealth Management, will lead the team from the city-state.

He took on the role recently in October, and will guide clients according to their specific circumstances and objectives, together with relationship managers, investment specialists and external professional advisers.

Portfolio sizes of clients typically start from US$5 million, as Schroders Wealth Management targets HNW and UHNW individuals and families.

But deconflicting with the firm’s main investment management business can be tricky. Hence, the wealth management business’ revenue model is “open architecture”, and primarily fee based, rather than balance-sheet or transaction-led, Schroders said.

“The objective is to build long-term, recurring revenues by growing and retaining client assets, rather than relying on lending spreads, product margins or transaction volumes,” the company noted.

Clients access the “lowest-fee share class” so they are not effectively paying both a wealth management fee and an additional distribution margin on the underlying Schroders product.

Strong investment governance and transparent fees will help with this alignment, too, the experts added.

More than a safe haven

Singapore’s reputation as a “safe haven” draws in many HNW and UHNW families to manage their wealth in a “stable” location, explained Tan. 

But she pointed out that over the years, the country has also evolved – now offering significant “international presence”.

This will benefit Schroders’ Asia wealth management hub based in Singapore, as it aims to foster tax transparency and strengthen global cooperation within the sector.

Serving families in Asia from the Republic will require more than “quick fixes” or a predetermined set of products moving forward, said Chiam – especially since they prioritise harmony and business continuity in wealth management.

The strategy is definitely not to “plug and play”, he warned – as the advisory does not advocate solutions focused solely on short-term gains.

“Throughout my career, I’ve seen different families set up certain structures just for the purpose of taking on tax advantages, which only tears them apart in the process,” said Chiam.

He said the advisory process at Schroders Wealth Management will therefore be customised to the long-term goals of each different family – for their wealth to endure across generations.

Singapore has seen significant growth in the number of family offices, with over 2,000 single-family offices here, according to Monetary Authority of Singapore data.

“Asian families tend to build their wealth through operating businesses, and so a family office is a (typical) operating model for their family wealth,” explained Chiam.

Tan said with this trend set to continue, the firm is keen to support family offices setting up in the city-state for the first time.

“Support in an integrated manner is something we can do…from assisting with the set-up itself, to wealth advisory and other investment portfolio work,” she noted.

How HNW families invest in Singapore, Hong Kong

Tan shared that a large proportion of their clients from the region will “play the field” by placing assets in both Singapore and Hong Kong.

“We see that increasingly, our clients with family offices want to book (their assets) in both locations in Asia, for different reasons,” she noted.

Fundamentally, Hong Kong offers a more direct gateway to Chinese and other North Asia equities, with capital markets there being more “robust”.

One of the families she worked with has family offices in Singapore and Hong Kong. She noted how the more conservative assets and traditional portfolios were booked in Singapore.

Meanwhile, the same family has “higher-risk assets” invested in Hong Kong.

The Asia CEO said clients generally want the best of worlds for their portfolios and wealth – meaning their approach to utilising the Asia hubs is more “complementary…than competitive”.

Schroders, which is primarily an investment manager, was acquired by American asset manager Nuveen on Oct 1. The combined entity is valued at US$2.6 trillion in assets across public and private markets.

Globally, the firm’s wealth management division manages £129.8 billion (US$172.9 billion) as at June this year.

data.title: Tokyo inflation accelerates, backing case for BOJ rate hike
data.description:
INFLATION in Japan’s capital city accelerated to the fastest pace this year, backing the case for a Bank of Japan rate increase next month as it focuses on keeping price growth around its 2 per cent target.

The consumer price index excluding fresh food rose 2.9 per cent in November from a year earlier in Tokyo, the highest level since July 2025, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications reported on Friday (Nov 27). The result matched the consensus forecast of economists.

Tokyo inflation is a leading indicator of nationwide price trends. The index that strips out both fresh food and energy, a gauge closely monitored by the BOJ as a measure of underlying inflation, climbed 2.5 per cent, while overall CPI rose 2.8 per cent.

Among factors driving gains were rising costs for electricity, up 9.5 per cent, and for city gas bills, which increased by almost 14 per cent.

In both cases, the figures reflect the impact of the end of subsidies on utility bills that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government rolled out for three months in the summer. Also, price gains for processed food accelerated a tad. 

Rice prices dropped almost 34 per cent, the biggest decline in the data going back to 1971. Rice, a daily staple for households, has become a major drag on CPI after being among primary drivers of overall inflation a year ago.

Friday’s CPI data add to recent signs of persistent price pressures and strengthen the case for the BOJ to raise interest rates next month.

The central bank has said its task is now to keep underlying inflation around the current level after reaching its target for the first time since the introduction of the goal in 2013.

Service prices — a key measure of the sustainability of inflation — increased 2.1 per cent from a year earlier, largely unchanged.

Takaichi last month announced plans to reinstate utility subsidies for three months starting in December.

She is also seeking to cut the sales tax on food from April to ease the cost-of-living burden on households. At the same time, the government will scale back gasoline subsidies. Together, those measures complicate the BOJ’s task of gauging underlying inflation.

Earlier this week, the BOJ’s consumer price indicator that subtracts the impact of temporary government steps accelerated to 3.5 per cent, the fastest pace in three years. Service prices charged among businesses also rose by the most in 36 years. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Human oversight in AI should be measured, not assumed
data.description:
RECENT reports in The Business Times have highlighted that clear permissions, audit trails, well-governed data and human sign-off on consequential decisions are key safeguards for financial institutions deploying artificial intelligence agents.

But keeping a human in the loop is not, by itself, a sufficient control. The more useful question is what risk that human checkpoint is meant to reduce, and whether it actually does so.

At the recent Global Finance & Technology Network session on AI innovation and governance, I asked a senior leader at a global bank whether an agent’s mandate could change in real time as conditions changed. The response was candid. It was a difficult question requiring further analysis.

That matters because human review can become a significant constraint as agentic workflows scale. McKinsey found that for a banking customer-service agent, human oversight accounted for 70 to 75 per cent of variable run costs, compared with 20 to 25 per cent for token costs.

The figures will differ across workflows, but they expose an important trade-off. Applying human approval too broadly can undermine the efficiency automation is meant to create.

Oversight should therefore follow the risk. A suspected fraud case, rejected loan, or large transfer to a new counterparty may warrant human judgment.

An agent assembling documents or updating an internal workflow within tightly defined permissions may not. The relevant factors include customer impact, value at risk, reversibility and uncertainty.

That principle is consistent with the AI risk-management guidelines from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), which urge financial institutions to apply controls proportionately according to their risk exposure and the scale and nature of their AI use.

MAS’ Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime Framework complements that direction with more granular guidance on how agent actions can be authorised, recorded and escalated for human review.

Banks should apply the same discipline to human oversight.

There is no single formula for assessing whether a checkpoint works. The industry will need evidence on where intervention catches material problems, changes proposed actions or adds delay without reducing risk.

A checkpoint may remain necessary for audit or accountability, even if interventions are rare.

The bank should be able to explain what risk it controls.

Crucially, this rule book cannot remain static. Agents act at machine speed, while the policies, mandates and controls governing them still change at human speed.

As agents take on new tasks, banks will need to revisit whether their escalation points still match the risks.

The goal is not maximum autonomy or maximum human involvement; it is to put human judgment where it changes the outcome. Every escalation should have a clear purpose.

Wei You Pan Field chief technology officer, MongoDB

data.title: Talks with US may result in 10-20% tariffs; trade-offs expected: Gan Kim Yong
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore has yet to begin negotiations on a new trade deal with the US, but will work with Washington to secure lower tariffs while helping affected businesses manage the impact of higher duties, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said on Thursday (Nov 26).

“The tariff is a surprise to us, and it’s not something that we expect from a major trading partner,” he noted.

Gan, who is also minister for energy, trade and industry (trade), was speaking to the media following a proposal by the US Trade Representative’s (USTR) office on Wednesday to impose tariffs of up to 20 per cent on Singapore and other trading partners, following a Section 301 probe into “unfair trading practices”.

Singapore will engage the US to understand the American government’s concerns, and establish whether such concerns can be addressed.

“If we are able to do so, we hope we look forward to lower tariffs,” Gan added.

Need for “give and take”

Tariffs imposed on Singapore under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, which is intended to address practices that Washington deems unfair to US commerce, now stand at 12.5 per cent, and the proposed new tariff would potentially raise the rate by 7.5 percentage points.

This rate could be lowered to 10 per cent if the city-state reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the US, or concludes other negotiations related to the latest findings.

Gan noted that negotiations with the US may result in a tariff rate “somewhere in between” 10 and 20 per cent, adding that the Republic must be willing to accept certain trade-offs in the negotiations. “There will be a give and take; there will be compromises.”

Besides securing a lower tariff rate, he pointed out that the Singapore government’s current priority is to help domestic companies manage the impact of tariffs.

The new tariffs will raise the effective tariff rate on Singapore goods from 7.8 to 10.3 per cent, which could affect about S$9.4 billion of Singapore exports to the US, he noted.

He added the government is working with the Singapore Economic Resilience Task Force – which was set up in April 2025, in part to help navigate the immediate uncertainties caused by US tariffs – to reach out to affected companies in order to manage this impact.

Claims of excess capacity

The USTR report cited several Singapore government policies that it claims create, sustain or contribute to “structural excess capacity and production”, which it said warrants the imposition of tariffs.

Alleging that the city-state produces more goods than it would under ordinary market conditions, the report identified Singapore’s “industrial planning apparatus” as a main underlying intervention leading to structural overcapacity.

It cited Singapore’s Manufacturing 2030 vision and Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2030 plan as the main policies indicative of such intervention.

Other policies cited by the report include Singapore’s compulsory savings schemes under the Central Provident Fund system, which require residents to contribute up to 20 per cent of their wages towards savings accounts.

“These contribution levels are far beyond those of the US and many developed economies,” said the USTR.

It argued that CPF contribution requirements suppress consumption levels and feed Singapore’s “large, persistent current account surplus”.

When asked, Gan told the press that he was “surprised” by the USTR’s comments on the CPF scheme, and noted that the scheme is both unique to Singapore and critical to its needs, particularly in ensuring Singaporeans are self-reliant in their retirement.

“It’s not a scheme to suppress domestic consumption,” he explained. “We will explain our position to them, and we hope that they will understand what CPF is about.”

Gan noted that the bilateral relationship between Singapore and the US remains multifaceted, extending beyond economics into other aspects.

“We hope to continue to strengthen our bilateral relationship, and we look forward to looking for a way to resolve differences,” he added.
